title: Direct-to-disc Larry Coryell recordings in Nashville
summary: Dan and Chris describe cutting a whole record side at once, the 'Midnight Sailor' takes ruined by a police car and Coryell's beer-bottle slide solo.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: only thing that was ever harder is we did some Larry Coryell recordings and that was direct to disc where they put a vinyl thing, they heat it up, they stick it on, they put a thing and they —

It goes literally right into the vinyl. And in fact two studios in Nashville were involved. So there was two side-by-side studios. See there are so many studios and one was like half a block from the other and the thing is going on.
Yeah but that’s crazy because you have to do a whole half of a record.
Yeah it’s not a tune at a time, it’s a whole side of a record at a time.
And so if you made a mistake it’s like ugh, you’ve got to go back and the guy’s got to heat up the vinyl you know. That process was terrible.

There’s a funny story that goes with that which is, and they’re actually really good records, but Darius had written a song called “The Midnight Sailor.” And that was the one that was the worst. Where it was never our fault, it was like one time a cop car went down the alley between the two. And like in the take it was like [speaks loudly as if with megaphone] “we’ve got a ten four five…” you know it was like oh, no. And it was 18 minutes into a beautiful performance of three tunes on one side. So that got scrapped. And another time like, “Oh we got a bump in the vinyl we’ve got to start again.” And each time this would happen Larry would, we’d take a break while they reset everything and he’d have another beer. So we’re finally into the fifth attempt at doing this whole side. And at that point when it comes to Larry’s guitar solo — he was very inventive — out comes the beer bottle and it’s become like a slide guitar thing with a Heineken beer bottle. And you could hear it to this day on that record. And it actually sounds kind of great.
